newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Jordan's Michael Collins film to open in Ireland.
newsitem.headline: Jordan's Michael Collins film to open in Ireland.

text.p: Neil Jordan's Michael Collins has its Irish premiere on Wednesday but the film, about the man who masterminded Ireland's fight for independence from British rule, has been embroiled in controversy before the credits even roll.

The $28 million Hollywood drama, which features Schindler's List star Liam Neeson as the charismatic Collins, claimed the best film and best actor awards at the Venice film festival where it received a 10-minute standing ovation.

But it has provoked fierce criticism and a heated debate closer to home where Jordan has been charged with historical inaccuracy and with inflaming passions at a sensitive time in the Northern Ireland peace process.
In a hard-hitting attack, leading Irish historian Paul Bew accused Jordan, who both wrote and directed the film, of "selective amnesia in pursuit of an unbending political agenda".
"Back to the Future it may be; history it ain't," Bew wrote in Britain's Daily Telegraph.
But Jordan, whose previous films include Interview with the Vampire and the Crying Game, has defended his work.
"It's not a work of history, it's not a historical document," he told an Irish film magazine. "The film is as accurate a dramatic reconstruction as I could make."
One of the most contentious scenes in the film shows a Belfast policeman blown up in a car bomb attack.

Historians point out that car bomb attacks, a feature of the recent violence in Northern Ireland, did not occur in the 1920s, A group representing disabled police officers in Northern Ireland described the scene as an insult to the memory of officers killed there.

The film has also been accused of offering encouragement to the Irish Republican Army (IRA), which is fighting British rule in Northern Ireland, and of inciting young people to violence at a critical time in the Northern Ireland peace process.

"It is anti-British in the extreme and is basically Provo (IRA) propaganda... Young, stupid men seeing this film with its tissue of lies and inaccuracies will be impelled to be angry at England," said Irish newspaper columnist Eoghan Harris, who has written a rival screenplay about the life of Collins.
But the film is not without its fans.
It has been warmly received by many film critics. One described it as "intelligent, stirring and noble". Another said it was "more likely to increase understanding than foment misunderstandings".
Ireland's film censor Sheamus Smith took the unprecedented step of praising the film as "a landmark in Irish cinema".
Smith awarded the film a "Parental Guidance" certificate -- a caution to families that they might not want their children to watch it.
He said that in spite of its crude language and scenes depicting cruelty and violence, he was not barring youngsters from seeing it because of its historical importance.
The film, which features Julia Roberts as Collins' girlfriend, seems certain to score at the Irish box office when it goes on general release on Friday.

"If interest before it opens is an indication of how it will do, there will be full houses everywhere," said Ita Bourke of Ward Anderson which runs a number of Irish cinemas. "It will probably be the biggest thing ever."
